value.overview: The Clay-colored Thrush (Turdus grayi), known as the yigüirro in Costa Rica, is a medium-sized, plain brown songbird of the thrush family. Its rich, varied song is one of the most familiar bird sounds in Costa Rica, where the species is the national bird. It is adaptable and commonly lives near people, using gardens, farms, coffee plantations, parks, forest edges, and open woodland rather than only remote natural forest.
value.classification: The Clay-colored Thrush belongs to the thrush family, Turdidae, in the order Passeriformes. It is one of several Central American Turdus thrushes.
value.identification: This robin-sized thrush is brown overall, usually with a slightly warmer or paler belly, faint streaking on the throat, orange-brown eyes, and a dull yellowish bill. The sexes look alike. Adults are generally 20.5–26.5 centimeters long. Juveniles have buffy markings on the wings and upperparts and darker spotting on the underparts. It often stays on the ground or in low vegetation, moving with short hops and frequently flicking its tail after landing.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America to northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica, it is widespread and familiar in nearly all regions, including the Central Valley, lowlands, foothills, and many settled areas. It uses open woodland, forest edges, shrubby growth, gardens, parks, orchards, pastures with trees, coffee plantations, and cultivated landscapes. It generally avoids extensive, undisturbed interior forest and is especially common where trees and dense vegetation occur close to human habitation.
value.migrationStatus: The Clay-colored Thrush is primarily resident in Costa Rica and is present there throughout the year. It does not undertake the long-distance seasonal migration typical of many northern thrushes, although local movements may occur in response to food, weather, or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica commonly coincides with the onset of the rainy or green season, with activity often concentrated from approximately April through June, although timing can vary. The female usually builds a sturdy cup nest of grasses, roots, moss, plant fibers, and mud. Nests are placed in trees, shrubs, epiphytes, on ledges, or occasionally on human structures. Clutches usually contain two or three pale blue to greenish-blue eggs marked with reddish brown. The species may raise more than one brood in a season.
value.dietFeeding: The Clay-colored Thrush is an opportunistic omnivore. It searches leaf litter and soil for insects, earthworms, and other invertebrates, and may also take small lizards or snakes. Fruit is an important food, especially when trees and shrubs are producing heavily. Individuals often forage alone or in pairs on the ground, but several may gather in fruiting trees. They may also capture flying termites or feed on prey disturbed by army ants.
value.behavior: This thrush is usually seen alone or in pairs, though small groups may gather at abundant fruit sources. It spends much time hopping across lawns, paths, leaf litter, and open ground while probing or turning leaves with its bill. Its song is a loud, musical series of varied phrases, and its common calls include soft chup notes. Pairs defend nests vigorously and may attack or mob potential predators. Both parents feed the young after hatching.

conservation.populationTrend: No meaningful global decline is established; available broad-scale monitoring indicates a generally stable to increasing population trend.
